content_voiceover: This slide presents the landmark SIPPET study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016, which compared inhibitor development rates between recombinant factor eight and plasma-derived factor eight in previously untreated patients with severe hemophilia A. The Kaplan-Meier curve tracks cumulative inhibitor development over fifty exposure days. Patients receiving recombinant factor eight, shown in gray, developed inhibitors at a substantially higher cumulative rate, plateauing around forty-five percent, compared to patients receiving plasma-derived factor eight, shown in black, which plateaued around twenty-seven percent. Both curves rise steeply within the first twenty exposure days, reflecting the fact that inhibitor development in previously untreated patients typically occurs early in treatment, then flattens as patients who haven't developed inhibitors by then are unlikely to do so later. SIPPET was practice-changing because it was the first randomized controlled trial to directly compare these product classes and found a statistically significant, roughly sixty percent higher relative risk of inhibitor development with recombinant factor eight, generating ongoing debate about product selection in previously untreated patients, especially given that plasma-derived products contain von Willebrand factor, which may play a protective, tolerogenic role.
keypoints: SIPPET was the first RCT comparing rFVIII versus pdFVIII in previously untreated hemophilia A patients
Recombinant FVIII: about 45 percent cumulative inhibitor development
Plasma-derived FVIII: about 27 percent cumulative inhibitor development
Most inhibitors developed within the first 20 exposure days
keypoint_voiceover: Key points from SIPPET. This was the first randomized controlled trial directly comparing recombinant and plasma-derived factor eight in previously untreated patients. Recombinant factor eight showed about forty-five percent cumulative inhibitor development, versus about twenty-seven percent with plasma-derived factor eight. And most inhibitor development happened early, within the first twenty exposure days, which is when previously untreated patients are most vulnerable.
